AA Insurance Board 
(the Board) 
The Board is the governance body responsible for overseeing climate-related risks and opportunities. 
It approves policies, risk appetite, strategy, metrics, targets, and external climate-related disclosures.  
It meets at least five times a year. 
Board sponsors
Directors Nadine Tereora and Jimmy Higgins act as an interface between Management and the Board,  
providing guidance and feedback on mandatory climate-related disclosures (CRD) matters.

reports from management concerning 
climate-related risks and opportunities 
in order to provide appropriate 
oversight of the assessment and 
management of such risks and 
opportunities. It also reviews and 
endorses our climate-related 
disclosures annually.
It meets at least five times a year. 
The Nominations Committee assesses 
Board composition by evaluating 
skills, experience, diversity and 
independence.
It meets at least twice a year. 
The PCR Committee assesses 
performance using a balanced 
scorecard that considers financial and 
non-financial measures, and monitors 
the effectiveness of our broader people 
and culture policies and practices.  
The balanced scorecard is used to 
assess Management’s incentive. At this 
stage, climate-related performance 
metrics are not incorporated into 
remuneration policies, but this is 
subject to ongoing review.
It meets at least four times a year.
The Investment Committee sets our 
investment guidelines and oversees the 
performance and management of our 
investments, including compliance with 
our Responsible Investment Policy.
It meets at least twice a year. 
Board level
Our Board is supported by a variety 
of Board level committees, each 
with distinct responsibilities as 
shown in table 2. 
Our Board members have complementary 
skillsets, experience and backgrounds. All 
members are experienced in operating in a 
rapidly changing regulatory environment 
and managing risks and opportunities during 
uncertainty. No single Director is responsible 
for a topic, rather the Board exercises its 
responsibilities collectively. 
A Board skills matrix is completed to 
review the individual and collective skills, 
knowledge and experience of Board members. 
Areas included in the matrix include risk 
management, corporate strategy and 
sustainability. The Nominations Committee 
assists in this assessment as well as evaluating 
the competencies and suitability of any 
prospective directors. 
Board members are provided with learning materials and climate education sessions 
where uplift opportunities are identified. This year, educational materials were provided 
to the Board covering changes to the CRD regime, Directors’ duties in relation to the CRD 
regime, an overview of the FMA’s December 2024 report ‘Climate-related Disclosures: 
Insights from our reviews’ and recommended key areas of focus for Directors in FY25. 
Management also held an important session with the Board to discuss and approve 
climate transition planning principles.

text:
Physical impacts
Transition impacts
The impacts of climate change 
can be physical (more frequent, 
severe weather events and longer-
term shifts in climate patterns) or 
transition (changes to the market, 
technology, policy or reputation 
because of the shift to a low 
emission economy). 
We have assessed whether we have 
experienced any physical or transition impacts 
from climate change during FY25, noting that 
it is often difficult to know whether impacts 
are definitively caused by climate change.
Our assessment involved a review of whether 
any anticipated climate-related impacts (as 
detailed on pages 12-14) materialised in the 
year. We analysed FY25 business performance 
data including claims costs, reinsurance 
premiums, policy numbers, cancellations 
trends and reputation indices and quantified 
the financial impacts where we judged these 
to be material.
Strategy
Current impacts of 
climate change
During FY25, we were not materially 
impacted by any changes related to the 
transition. Whilst our exposure to electric 
vehicles (EVs) is increasing, this is not having 
a material impact on our claims costs or cycle 
times, and we continue to see growth in our 
motor portfolio.
During FY25, we experienced five weather-
related natural hazard events, which we define 
as events with expected customer claims of 
more than $1.5m. We estimate that the total 
claims cost from these events will be around 
$19.7m, up from $6.2m in FY24, a relatively 
benign year with only two weather-related 
natural hazard events. 
For context, over the last 20 years we have 
averaged around three weather-related natural 
hazard events per year. Once adjusted for 
inflation and growth, the 20-year average 
claims costs in relation to these events is 
$29.3m per year, however this is heavily 
skewed by the 2023 North Island Weather 
Events. If excluded, the average is around 
$16.4m per year, which has been gradually 
rising. Whilst we cannot attribute these 
increases to climate change with certainty, 
climate change is expected to increase the 
frequency and severity of weather events and 
therefore may be responsible for the long-term 
average increase in weather-related claims. 
The reinsurance premiums that we pay 
have stabilised in FY25 after increasing 
significantly in FY24 in the aftermath of the 
2023 North Island Weather Events. Whilst 
the increase from FY24 is negligible, these 
costs have risen by $64.6m, more than 200%, 
since FY22. Whilst some of this increase is 
due to policy growth, our average reinsurance 
premium on a per policy basis has increased 
by 170% between FY22 and FY25. These 
increased reinsurance premiums represent a 
significant increase in costs to the business 
each year.

Strategy
Climate change scenario analysis (continued) 
Transition analysis
The analysis of physical impacts looked 
at how our view of risk, measured through 
Average Annual Loss (AAL), might change in 
the short, medium and long terms under the 
three scenarios. AAL is the average financial 
loss we expect in a year for an insured risk 
or portfolio due to damage from weather 
events, which can be modelled based on the 
projected temperature changes defined by the 
equivalent SSP. 
We analysed our present-day home, contents, 
motor and small business insurance portfolios 
and overlaid climate models for flood, storm 
and coastal inundation. Further details behind 
the modelling methods, assumptions and 
limitations can be found in Appendix 2. 
The analysis concluded that AALs are projected 
to increase under each scenario due to the 
increased frequency of severe weather events. 
Increases to AALs are predominantly due to 
flooding and coastal inundation, whereas the 
AALs for storm are not projected to change 
materially under the three scenarios. 
We used economic modelling to identify 
and assess risks and opportunities that 
could arise due to the economic impacts of 
climate change, including due to the net zero 
transition. The assessment was performed for 
each of the three scenarios and looked at the 
potential flow on impacts to our investment 
portfolio and on insurance affordability. 
Further details behind the modelling methods, 
assumptions and limitations can be found in 
Appendix 2. 
Under each scenario, insurance affordability 
for New Zealanders is projected to get tighter 
over time. The disorderly scenario is projected 
to see the greatest stress on affordability 
of the three scenarios, with projected high 
inflation and financial instability caused 
by a delayed yet aggressive shift towards 
sustainability. 
The transition risk within our investment 
portfolio was assessed as relatively low 
(around 5%) due to the low level of equity 
exposure in the portfolio and the nature of 
those investments.

During the year we have been 
working to further reduce our 
operational emissions as covered 
by our short-term emissions 
reduction target.
Between FY20 and FY25, we have reduced the 
operational emissions covered by our FY30 
42% reduction target by 21.3% (see page 25 
for further detail). 
During FY25, we assessed our vehicle fleet, 
which was made up of 45 hybrids and two 
personal ICE vehicles, on a case-by-case basis 
to determine if any could be converted to EVs 
or retired from the fleet. In FY25, we removed 
31 hybrid vehicles and both ICE vehicles, 22 
of which were replaced by EVs. Most vehicle 
retirements took place in the latter half of the 
financial year, meaning our fuel emissions 
do not yet fully reflect the impact of these 
changes, but we expect to see decreasing fuel 
use from FY26.
We are also closely monitoring air travel, which 
began to rise after the end of the COVID-19 
pandemic. Last year, we introduced stricter 
permissions for approving business flights, and 
air travel emissions fell in FY25 compared to 
FY24. Whilst we plan to meet our FY30 target 
through fleet conversion, we are also relying on 
air travel not increasing significantly.  
Pillar 1: 'Decarbonising the entity'
A large portion of flights in FY25 related to a 
large scale but short term technology project, 
meaning there is scope to further reduce our 
air travel emissions going forwards. 
Currently our business model and strategy 
have not changed and are not planned to 
change to meet our current decarbonisation 
target, which we believe can be met through 
operational changes rather than fundamental 
strategic changes. We plan to meet this target 
by replacing our hybrid vehicle fleet with EVs, 
whilst closely monitoring air travel. Most of the 
fleet was converted in FY25, however further 
conversions have been budgeted for in FY26. 
Achievement of this target is partially 
dependent on the stability of emissions 
factors, which are outside our control. This 
includes the emissions factors associated with 
the fuel and electricity we use, both directly 
and indirectly. We also understand that 
travel is sometimes required where in-person 
engagement is essential to ensure successful 
outcomes, therefore further reductions to air 
travel emissions will depend on balancing these 
needs with our emissions reduction target.
We currently do not have a long-term 
emissions reduction target as we are still 
working to gather data and measure our 
full scope 3 emissions baseline. Future 
decarbonisation strategies will be assessed 
in line with our climate transition planning 
guiding principles and any impacts on 
our business model and strategy will be 
communicated in future reports.

Our strategy and the way we 
operate is changing in response 
to climate-related risks and 
opportunities, key elements of 
which are detailed below, noting 
this is not an exhaustive list  
of responses. 
The main physical risks that we face stem 
from increasingly severe and frequent weather 
events affecting our customers’ assets that 
we have insured. A key aspect of our strategy 
is to understand and balance our portfolio of 
risks, so that we are not disproportionately 
affected when events occur and can continue 
to meet the needs of our customers when they 
make a claim. We have invested in third party 
models and address level data, which allowed 
us to introduce risk-based pricing for flooding 
in FY24 and begin working on the introduction 
of risk-based pricing for storm, which we 
expect to introduce in the future. We have 
also reassessed our underwriting strategy 
to pause offering new home insurance cover 
where we have reached a certain level of 
exposure in a higher risk area. Whilst we do 
not take decisions like this lightly, it is key 
to ensuring we can deliver on our promise of 
caring, helping and getting things sorted for 
our existing customers. 
Pillar 2: 'Responding to the entity’s climate-related risks and opportunities'
To respond to the transition risk around 
mobility trends, we are focused on re-
balancing our product portfolio, including 
growing our market share of home and 
contents policies. We also closely monitor 
our number of motor vehicle policies 
and market share each month, alongside 
investing in customer research to understand 
changing market trends, in order to monitor 
any changes to the motor vehicle market 
that could indicate personal motor vehicle 
ownership is declining.
Both physical and transition impacts of 
climate change are expected to have an 
impact on insurance affordability, for both us 
as a business and for our customers. We are 
working to improve efficiency and reduce our 
own costs per policy, which is a contributing 
factor when determining pricing, although 
this is not solely in response to climate 
change. A key strategic development this 
year was the opening of a second Drive Group 
site in Auckland, bringing the total to two 
key locations across the region. Drive Group 
offers vehicle repair services and adds valuable 
repair capacity to the market. In recent years, 
we have experienced significant policy growth, 
requiring scalable and innovative solutions. 
This collaboration strengthens our ability to 
meet rising customer demand. 
We remain focused on building strong 
partnerships - including with Drive Group and 
our wider quality repairer network - to deliver 
efficient, customer-focused outcomes through 
collaboration and operational resilience.

the economy wide transition, we 
do not expect our business model 
to fundamentally change. We 
continue to focus on helping our

who are now seeing the risk at their address 
more accurately reflected in their premiums.

a high level through customer renewal notices, 
and our frontline teams have been provided

contact us for more detailed information. We 
also provide education about natural hazards 
as part of our community engagement and 
social impact programmes, including with 
the Student Volunteer Army. Through this 
partnership and others, we are working to 
raise awareness and support New Zealanders 
to adapt and respond well to any climate risks 
that they may face. 
Pillar 3: 'Contributing to an economy‑wide transition'
We understand that we can support customers 
further through offering products and 
propositions that support climate resilience. 
Since FY24, we have been focused on a 
multi‑year transformation programme to 
modernise our core systems, enhance the 
customer experiences we deliver, and improve 
our ability to meet changing customer needs 
over time. Our refreshed strategy aims to reap 
the benefits of this significant investment. 
Our existing motor products already cover EVs, 
however further opportunities exist to create 
competitive sustainability linked products 
and propositions, including those which could 
improve resilience to weather events. These 
are in consideration for our future roadmap, 
once capability becomes available.
We regularly advocate for climate resilience 
and adaptation at a government, local 
government, and community level. Our 
engagement with central government is 
often in collaboration with Suncorp New 
Zealand, where we put forward a joint voice 
on measures we believe are important to 
help protect New Zealanders from the worst 
impacts of climate change, and to ensure that 
the private general insurance market remains 
financially robust, so we can be here for our 
customers in the long term. 
Our local government engagement is focused 
on many of these same objectives, as well 
as hearing from those on the ground around 
the country, ensuring that we are informed, 
and our actions are representative of our 
customers’ needs. We are also active within 
the financial services sector, for example with 
the ICNZ, and participate in their education 
and advocacy discussions and consultations. 
At a community level, we have various 
partnerships that focus on natural disaster 
response and recovery, which we have built 
into our Major Event Response plans. This 
year we developed a Customer Response 
Team, which is responsible for on-the-ground 
insurance support for customers after a  
major event. 
We welcomed the Independent Reference 
Group’s Climate Adaptation Report and

shaping a resilient future for New Zealand. We 
look forward to engaging constructively in the 
legislative process upon the introduction of 
the proposed adaptation framework to New 
Zealand Parliament.

Risk Management
Our risk management model 
We employ a ‘three lines of defence’ model across 
our business to manage the accountabilities and 
governance arrangements for the management of risk: 
The following documents and tools 
guide how we identify, assess and 
manage risk: 
Our Risk Management Programme - 
Our Risk Management Programme (RMP) 
sets our approach to identify, assess and 
manage our risks, and the way these risks are 
recorded, reported and escalated within our 
organisation. The RMP is supported by more 
specific standards and frameworks, including 
our Risks, Obligations, and Controls Self-
Assessment (ROCSA) Standard, which helps 
us identify and assess risks and compliance 
obligations in a structured way. The RMP 
categorises our risks into strategic disruption 
risks, strategic execution risks, financial risks, 
insurance risks or operational (including 
compliance) risks. See table 6 on the following 
page for more detail on these different types 
of risks. 
Our Risk Appetite Statement - Our Board 
sets and approves our Risk Appetite Statement 
(RAS) outlining the nature and level of risk, 
including climate risk, that it is willing to 
accept in pursuit of our strategic objectives. 
We escalate risks that are ‘outside of appetite’ 
to Risk Committee and BARCC and monitor 
them until we bring them ‘within appetite’. 
In FY25, our climate transition planning 
principles were incorporated into the RAS. 
Our risk management system - We record all 
material risks, excluding strategic disruption 
risks, in our Integrated Risks, Issues, Incidents 
System (IRIIS). We use IRIIS to log incidents 
and record and monitor action plans, risks, 
controls and obligations. IRIIS is not used 
to record longer term strategic disruption 
risks, including the climate-related risks and 
opportunities identified through CCSA, however 
shorter term operational impacts stemming 
from climate-related risks may be recorded in 
IRIIS where material. 
We do not exclude any part of our value 
chain when identifying, assessing and 
managing our risks, including climate-
related risks, and do not have a process 
for prioritising climate-related risks 
relative to any other types of risks.

Physical risks
The material physical climate-related risks 
stem from increasingly severe and frequent 
weather events affecting our customers 
and the assets we insure, particularly 
from flooding. Therefore, to understand 
the extent to which we are vulnerable to 
physical risk, we analysed address level 
data to understand the portion of our home 
and contents portfolios that are deemed 
high or very high risk2 of flooding3. We 
considered but ultimately excluded our 
motor portfolio as the impact was deemed 
immaterial. 
As at 13 May 2025, 4.2% of our home 
and contents portfolios were classed as 
either at high risk or at very high risk of 
flooding. As per the transition planning 
section of this report, we are working to 
ensure we maintain a fair and balanced 
portfolio of risk and we are committed 
to ongoing education and engagement 
to help stakeholders understand why 
this is a critical step in upholding our 
responsibilities as a trusted insurer. 
Transition risks
The transition risks we face stem from 
a variety of drivers, including market 
conditions and changing consumer 
preferences. Potential inflationary 
pressures, the flow on impact on 
affordability of insurance, and the 
anticipated electrification of assets 
could impact all portfolios, whereas the 
anticipated decline in personal vehicle 
ownership is specific to our motor portfolio.
As at 30 June 2025, 55.9% of our total gross 
written premium was derived from personal 
motor policies. We do not expect the whole 
portfolio to be vulnerable to transition risk as 
New Zealanders will continue to need a range 
of transport options, which will likely require 
insurance. There is not yet reliable data to 
estimate what portion of New Zealand’s 
personal motor vehicle fleet will be impacted 
by changing mobility trends, therefore a 
more specific metric will be considered for 
future reports.
Opportunities
A key opportunity we face is to provide 
climate and sustainability linked products 
and propositions for our customers. During 
FY25 we have been focused on a core 
systems transformation that should allow 
the business more flexibility in product 
and proposition development in the future, 
although we are still defining our priorities 
and roadmap at this stage. 
We already insure EVs, with our EV 
exposure4 sitting at 3.2% of the motor 
portfolio between January and April 2025. 
This exposure includes battery electric 
vehicles and plug-in hybrids.
Capital deployed
During FY25 we deployed $1.56m towards 
climate transition planning activities 
including understanding and responding 
to climate-related risks and opportunities. 
This includes both operational and 
capital expenditure on key areas such 
as transitioning our fleet vehicles to EVs, 
address level modelling and data, natural 
hazards awareness, community resilience 
partnerships, customer research and 
consultancy costs.
This metric is limited to spend which can 
be directly attributable to responding to 
climate change. It does not include spend 
that was deployed for a separate business 
reason, but indirectly helps with our climate 
change response, for example efficiency 
improvements. It also does not include any 
salary cost attribution.
Beyond these, we do not currently use any other climate‑related 
metrics or KPIs within our business. We do not use an internal 
emissions price, and we have not linked management remuneration

Appendix 1: Full scenario narratives 
The disorderly scenario assumes that climate action is delayed 
initially, but changes in weather around the world results in a rapid 
shift so that sudden and uncoordinated transformation takes place. 
The scenario assumes a warming trajectory that stays below 2.0°C. 
From a social perspective, the uncoordinated and rapid shift results 
in a wider gap between rich and poor, and between urban and 
rural. Expectations for the role of insurers increase. Technology for 
mitigation and adaptation improves rapidly after 2030, but at high 
cost. The economic cost is high; while government is focused on the 
transition, the blunt nature of policies implemented increases many 
costs for businesses.
The hot house scenario assumes that current policy settings 
continue until 2100, leading to uncontrolled warming of at least 
3.0°C. From a social perspective, communities fracture and 
geopolitical tensions rise; populations focus on access to basic 
needs. Technology improves but continues to be focused on 
extraction and adaptation rather than transition. Governments 
invest in education and health, but the physical impacts of climate 
change severely damage many sectors and supply chains.
The orderly scenario is an ambitious and coordinated transition 
scenario with a warming trajectory limited to 1.5°C. From a social 
perspective, this scenario represents a coordinated and inclusive 
world that prioritises human and environmental wellbeing. 
Technology for mitigation and adaptation improves rapidly, and 
its uptake is supported through government policy. The economic 
impact is mixed, with some sectors (such as fossil fuels) shrinking 
and others (such as horticulture) growing in response to the 
changing world.

Scenario Narrative
Government policy on mitigation remains consistent throughout the 2020s before, in 2030, a record 
year for weather events globally, coupled with an alignment of political views, drives a global political 
shift. Governments around the world quickly commit to meaningful action on climate change, 
including in New Zealand.
Rapid reductions in emissions are necessary to meet the Paris Agreement temperature goals. This is a 
disruptive transition with insufficient consultation with the insurance and other critical sectors.
Conversations about expanding the NHC continue without action through the 2020s, before 
affordability concerns and a significant flood event in 2030 prompts the Government to rapidly 
expand the scheme’s coverage, and a new flood levy is introduced. This flood levy captures some of 
the market historically held by home insurers. Reinsurers withdraw in some regions, and some are 
unable to offer cover for lower layers.
The disruptive transition creates uncertainty for insurance companies. In particular, the EV transition 
becomes inevitable as emissions pricing and ICE vehicle running costs increase. But, in the sudden 
rush for EVs and electrification globally, inflation rises. By 2035, many households find the costs 
of running ICE vehicles expensive, and nor can they afford to purchase a new EV. Some households 
drop their insurance. At the same time, supply chains, parts and materials become very expensive as 
freight restrictions tighten and extreme weather events worsen. 
The rural sector is considered by some to be high-emitting and overpriced, while rural communities 
see corporate New Zealand as out of touch with rural issues. Some corporates are dragged into 
this dichotomy as they are torn between customer expectations of them to help homes invest 
in electrification and rising costs of repair, increasing extreme weather risk and inflation, and 
catastrophe-driven increases in reinsurance prices.
Scenario Narrative
Government action globally remains at the levels of the early 2020s, and global emissions continue to 
rise inexorably, even while New Zealand’s emissions fall.
The intensification of severe weather events is such that, by 2035, insurance in parts of New Zealand 
becomes very expensive. In response to this, the New Zealand Government focuses on strong 
adaptation policy. This includes an expansion of the NHC to cover most perils, taking a historically 
large market away from general insurers.
Reinsurers withdraw from covering certain perils in the New Zealand market. The withdrawal of 
reinsurance, which is driven partly by increasing risks in New Zealand and partly by uncertainty in key 
overseas markets, means some insurers cannot provide cover in certain areas anymore. Insurers write 
more innovative products.
Where coverage is still provided, costs are very high, and customers are frustrated. In this world, 
everything is expensive, and affordability is challenging in certain demographics.
This is a fractured world with global conflicts over water and food shortages, and energy security. 
By 2050, climate change is a significant driver of migration, and a large number of people see New 
Zealand’s (comparably) pleasant climate as an ideal destination. The influx of immigrants leads 
to vibrant communities in some areas and unrest in others. For insurers, the main focus becomes 
working together to get the government support they need to provide coverage to the increasingly at-
risk communities across the country.
Scenario Narrative
Government action to reduce emissions is strong, clear and consistent across the economy. New 
policies are introduced to accelerate emissions reductions, including incentives on the uptake of 
electric vehicles and home electrification, which create significant structural change to the economy. 
Despite being highly consequential, policies are designed in consultation with key sectors and 
stakeholders, creating a sense of inclusivity, and implementation is supported so industries can 
manage the transition.
The National Direction on Natural Hazard Decision-making is implemented in mid-2025, which gives 
councils the tools they need to effectively identify, measure and manage climate risks. By 2030, 
home insurers are put under pressure as they are expected to play a stronger role in protecting homes 
from climate impacts. Systems must be updated quickly to accommodate this additional risk and 
competition in the market for innovative products grows.
ICE vehicles are practically gone from the light vehicle fleet by 2040. The changing risk profile of 
electric homes and vehicles makes historically profitable portfolios demand a new approach. This 
gives an opportunity for new entrants into the market and fuels further competition. Certain insurers 
risk falling behind due to their slow innovation and uptake of new technologies.
Physical impacts worsen, but outcomes are not as severe as they might have been without climate 
action. Sea level rise, however, is partly locked in. There are some isolated affordability issues in 
the most exposed areas. Generally, these issues are manageable and only occur in certain areas. 
Reinsurance is therefore accessible for the New Zealand market, albeit at an increased price.

Appendix 2: CCSA modelling methods, assumptions and limitations 
Physical modelling
We used the third-party modelling expertise of both Finity (storm and coastal inundation modelling) and Aon (river and surface water flood modelling, as used in 2023). In scope portfolios were our home, 
contents, motor and small business insurance portfolios, as at 30 June 2024, assumed to be an appropriate proxy for present day. 
The modelling included matching address level portfolio data to third-party proprietary databases and applying a series of climate layers corresponding to the three chosen scenarios and time horizons. 
The AAL outputs were compared to our present day AAL to understand how these expected losses may change under different future climate scenarios. Results were summarised at a postcode level, but 
modelling was conducted at address level. 
The climate models used have significant assumptions and limitations, noting that different climate models can produce very different outcomes. The results are subject to high uncertainty and it is 
possible that the actual physical impacts of climate change will be materially different to those modelled. Nevertheless, the analysis provides useful insights into how risks could reasonably be expected 
to change in the future. The models used in this analysis are deemed appropriate as they are widely used in the insurance sector for understanding physical risks. We will continue to explore a range of 
models whilst in the exploratory phase of physical climate modelling. Some significant assumptions and limitations include: 
•	
The modelling projects the average of the range of possible losses each year, rather than losses associated with extreme tail events only. This means that individual extreme events are averaged within 
the AALs used; 
•	
The analysis excluded perils such as coastal erosion, wildfire, drought and rain induced landslip that could increase the expected losses from climate impacts due to quality model availability; 
•	
The analysis does not take into account any changes to our portfolio or strategy in the future in response to the anticipated physical impacts of climate change. 
Transition modelling
The transition modelling performed by Finity used a Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model created by Victoria University (Melbourne) to capture regional and national changes in response to 
potential economic shocks under each of the chosen scenarios. These were translated into an assessment of affordability (expected regional financial margins) and investments portfolio vulnerability 
(industry revenue growth by sector). 
Financial margins (household disposable income minus non-discretionary expenditure) were based on historical data from Stats NZ projected forwards using assumptions for inflation, wage growth and 
cost growth. The assessment was not based on any data specific to our business, rather the impacts were projected for New Zealand as a whole. For the investment portfolio analysis, our portfolio data was 
provided as at 30 June 2024, as a proxy for present day. Each counterparty was mapped to an industry sector and the projected revenue growth of each sector was compared to New Zealand GDP growth 
under each of the modelled scenarios. This gives an idea of how different industries may perform in relation to each other and identify whether our portfolio could be vulnerable. 
Economic models are highly uncertain as the dynamics of complex systems are extremely difficult to model, therefore results should be interpreted with caution. Due to this, the actual impacts of the 
climate transition could be materially different to those presented. Nevertheless, this analysis provides insights into how transition risks could affect our business. The models used in this analysis are 
deemed appropriate as they are widely used in the insurance sector for understanding transition risks. We will continue to explore a range of models whilst in the exploratory phase of transition risk 
modelling. Some significant assumptions and limitations include: 
•	
The model is based on simplified assumptions, including extrapolated historical data. These inputs may not change in a predictable or linear way into the future; 
•	
The model assumes households and businesses will act in an economically rationale way; 
•	
The model is limited in that it does not take into account the possibility of emerging industries in New Zealand, meaning the results are likely to be negatively biased.
